title: Integral full-rank lattice presentation of a finite fraction-field submodule
statement: Let $R$ be a commutative integral domain with fraction field $K$, let $r\ge0$, and let $M\subseteq K^r$ be an $R$-submodule spanned by finitely many vectors. There exist an integer $s\le r$, an $R$-submodule $N\subseteq R^s$, and $0\ne d\in R$ such that $dR^s\subseteq N$ and $M\cong N$ as $R$-modules.

source.place: Algebra, Tag 00PE (lemma-finite-length), proof: reduction to the K-span and the finite-case clearing of denominators, including a nonzero d with dR^s contained in the integral lattice

proof.text: Let V be the K-span of M. Set s = finrank_K V, which is at most r. Inclusion into V followed by a finite basis coordinate equivalence gives an injective R-linear map f:M→K^s. Its range P is finitely generated, isomorphic to M, and spans K^s. The span_range_inclusion_eq_top and map_span lemmas establish the spanning assertion.

Choose finitely many generators of P. IsLocalization.exist_integer_multiples_of_finite on their coordinate pairs supplies a common nonzero denominator a. Let μ multiply vectors by a, and let ι:R^s→K^s be the coordinate algebra map. The generator calculation and span_le show μ(P)⊆range ι. Set N=ι^{-1}(μ(P)). Both maps are injective; map_comap_eq and equivMapOfInjective give P≅N.

For any vector in span_K P, a nonzero R-multiple belongs to P. Prove this by closure_induction: for a K-multiple of an element of P clear its scalar denominator using IsFractionRing.div_surjective; for a sum multiply the two denominators; zero uses 1. Apply this to each standard basis vector. The product of their nonzero denominators times a is nonzero d. The erased-product formula shows d times each integral basis vector belongs to N; summing the coordinates gives dR^s⊆N. Empty sums and products also prove the s=0 case.
